def: Plant breeding is the science of improving crop plants by selecting and combining desirable traits to develop new, superior varieties with higher yield, disease resistance or better quality.
points: Selection: choosing naturally occurring superior plants and propagating them further.
Hybridization: crossing two genetically different plants to combine desirable traits of both parents in the offspring.
Mutation breeding: using radiation or chemicals to induce useful mutations for new traits.
Breeders aim for traits like higher yield, disease resistance, drought tolerance and better nutritional quality.
New varieties are tested over several generations before being released for farming.
Plant breeding has given high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice, central to the Green Revolution.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Select parent plants with good traits"] --> B["Hybridization or mutation"]
  B --> C["Select best offspring"]
  C --> D["Test over generations"]
  D --> E["Release new variety"]

example: Dwarf wheat varieties developed through plant breeding resist lodging (falling over) and gave much higher yields during the Green Revolution.
tip: Name all three methods (selection, hybridization, mutation breeding) with one line each — questions often ask to 'enlist' methods.

def: The Green Revolution was a period of major increase in agricultural production in India (1960s-70s) achieved through high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, fertilizers, irrigation and modern farming techniques.
points: It was led by scientists like Dr. M.S. Swaminathan, using HYV seeds of wheat and rice developed from dwarf varieties.
Key inputs were: HYV seeds, chemical fertilizers, pesticides, assured irrigation, and better farm machinery.
It made India self-sufficient in food grain production, turning it from a food-importing to food-exporting nation.
Dwarf varieties resisted lodging (falling due to heavy grain) and gave higher yields per acre.
Negative effects included soil degradation, loss of soil fertility over time, and reduced crop diversity.
Overuse of chemical fertilizers and pesticides also caused water pollution and health issues.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["HYV seeds introduced"] --> B["Fertilizers and irrigation added"]
  B --> C["Crop yield increases sharply"]
  C --> D["India becomes food self-sufficient"]

example: India's wheat production increased several times after introducing dwarf HYV wheat varieties in Punjab and Haryana during the 1960s.
tip: Mention one benefit and one drawback of the Green Revolution — balanced answers score full marks in evaluative questions.

def: Animal husbandry is the scientific management and breeding of livestock (cattle, poultry, fish) for improved production of milk, meat and other products; dairy management specifically focuses on improving milk yield and quality from cattle.
points: Dairy management includes selecting high-yielding breeds, proper feeding, housing, and disease control.
Cross-breeding of local cattle with exotic breeds (like Jersey, Holstein-Friesian) improves milk yield while retaining disease resistance of local breeds.
Artificial insemination (AI) is used to breed cows with semen from superior bulls without natural mating.
Proper nutrition (balanced fodder with proteins, minerals) is essential for high milk production.
Regular health checks and vaccination prevent diseases that reduce productivity.
Clean housing and milking hygiene prevent contamination and increase milk quality.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Select high yielding breed"] --> B["Cross breeding or AI"]
  B --> C["Balanced feed and housing"]
  C --> D["Health care and vaccination"]
  D --> E["Higher quality milk yield"]

example: Crossing local Indian cattle with Holstein-Friesian bulls through artificial insemination has significantly increased milk yield in India's dairy farms.
tip: Mention artificial insemination specifically — it is a commonly tested keyword in animal husbandry questions.

def: Poultry farming is the practice of raising domesticated birds like chickens, ducks and turkeys for egg and meat production through scientific management of breeding, feeding and disease control.
points: Poultry birds are classified as layers (for egg production) and broilers (for meat production).
Cross-breeding of local and foreign breeds increases both egg-laying capacity and meat quality.
Proper housing with ventilation and controlled temperature improves bird health and productivity.
Balanced feed with proteins and vitamins improves growth rate and egg quality.
Vaccination programs protect poultry from diseases like Ranikhet disease and fowl pox.
Hygienic management of the poultry farm reduces disease spread and improves overall yield.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Select layer or broiler breed"] --> B["Balanced feed and housing"]
  B --> C["Vaccination against disease"]
  C --> D["Increased egg or meat yield"]

example: Broiler chickens are bred and managed to reach market weight in just 6-7 weeks due to optimized feed and breeding practices.
tip: Clearly differentiate 'layers' (eggs) from 'broilers' (meat) — this basic distinction is commonly asked.

def: Single Cell Protein (SCP) refers to protein-rich biomass obtained from microorganisms (bacteria, yeast, algae, fungi) cultured on cheap substrates, used as an alternative protein source for humans and animals.
points: SCP is produced by growing microorganisms like Spirulina (algae) or yeast on substrates such as molasses, whey or agricultural waste.
It is rich in protein, vitamins and minerals, making it a good food/feed supplement.
SCP production requires less land and water compared to conventional livestock farming.
Microorganisms multiply very fast, so SCP can be produced in large quantities quickly.
It helps solve food and protein shortage problems, especially in protein-deficient regions.
SCP is used as cattle feed supplement and sometimes as a human food additive.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Cheap substrate: molasses or whey"] --> B["Microorganism grown: yeast, algae, bacteria"]
  B --> C["Biomass harvested and processed"]
  C --> D["Protein-rich SCP food/feed"]

example: Spirulina, a blue-green alga, is commercially cultured and sold as a protein and vitamin supplement for both humans and animal feed.
tip: Give one example organism (Spirulina or yeast) with its use — examiners expect a concrete example, not just the definition.

def: Tissue culture (micropropagation) is a technique of growing a large number of genetically identical plants from a small piece of plant tissue (explant) under sterile, controlled laboratory conditions.
points: A small piece of plant tissue (explant) is placed on a nutrient medium containing hormones, sugars and minerals.
This medium induces the explant cells to divide and form an unorganized mass of cells called callus.
The callus is then treated with specific hormones to differentiate into shoots and roots, forming a complete plantlet.
The whole process is carried out under sterile (aseptic) conditions to avoid contamination.
Plantlets produced are genetically identical to the parent plant (clones).
This method allows rapid, large-scale multiplication of disease-free, high-quality plants (e.g., orchids, bananas).
formula: Explant -> Callus -> Shoot and root differentiation -> Plantlet

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Explant from parent plant"] --> B["Placed on nutrient medium"]
  B --> C["Callus forms"]
  C --> D["Shoots and roots differentiate"]
  D --> E["New plantlet, genetically identical"]

example: Banana plants are commercially micropropagated through tissue culture to produce thousands of disease-free, uniform plantlets from a single parent plant.
tip: Use the keyword 'callus' and mention 'aseptic/sterile conditions' — these two terms are essential for full marks.
